A metal fabricator and manufacturer entered into a contract for the sale of a plasma cutter made by the manufacturer. While the manufacturer had several plasma cutters on hand, the contract provided for the sale of a particular plasma cutter identified by its serial number. The contract specified that the manufacturer would ship the cutter by a third-party carrier. However, the contract did not specify who was to pay the costs of transportation nor the place of tender for the plasma cutter. The manufacturer shipped the cutter identified in the contract to the fabricator via a carrier under a proper contract for its transportation. The carrier delivered the cutter to the fabricator, and the fabricator verified that the cutter delivered was the one specified in the contract.
Under these facts, when did the risk of loss pass to the fabricator?

On October 30, a customer entered a retail beauty supply store to purchase hair dye to color her hair for Halloween. The clerk who helped the customer was hired the previous day and was not trained regarding different types of dye. The customer explained that she wanted a washable dye, as she had a presentation the following day at work and needed to look professional for it. The clerk showed the customer a permanent hair dye, assuring the customer that the dye was appropriate for her needs. The clerk then told the customer that because the dye was on sale, it was being sold "as is," and that she could not be responsible for any adverse reactions. The customer made the purchase and used the dye to color her hair. The customer could not wash out the dye from her hair on the morning of November 1. As a consequence, the customer lost an account because she could not deliver the presentation.
In a breach-of-warranty action against the store, will the customer likely prevail?

In the spring, a scholarship program held a competition to award $10,000 to the high school senior who wrote and submitted the best essay, as judged by the program's grading rubric. The competition announcement provided that any student could enter the contest by submitting an essay and a signed copy of the competition's "Terms and Conditions." Many students submitted essays, and the scholarship program selected a winner in accordance with their grading rubric the following fall. However, when the winning student tried to claim the award, the program refused to give it to him. The "Terms and Conditions" of the competition provided that the winner of the competition could receive the award only if he or she was enrolled in a public university in that state by the following fall. The winning student had not read the "Terms and Conditions" of the competition when he signed and submitted them with his essay and had already enrolled in an out-of-state private college by the fall.
If the winning student sues the scholarship program to recover the $10,000 award, will he succeed?

Before the season began, a professional hockey player entered into a signed, written agreement with the owner of the team. Among the provisions in the agreement was one that provided that, if the player scored 20 or more goals during the season, he would receive additional compensation. The player tried his best during the season but only managed to score 19 goals. The owner refused to pay the player any additional compensation.
Is the owner excused from paying the additional compensation?

In late March, a jeweler contracted to create and sell a ruby ring to a buyer on May 1. In early April, the price of rubies rose by 25%, and the jeweler could not purchase a ruby without losing money on the transaction. However, the jeweler had an emerald that was purchased for another customer who had canceled the order. The jeweler created the ring for the buyer using the emerald. On May 1, the jeweler tendered the emerald ring to the buyer in good faith, explaining the situation and pointing out that the emerald ring was the same value that the ruby ring would have been. The buyer refused to accept the emerald ring and refused to pay the jeweler the contract price.
Which of the following most accurately describes the legal relationship between the jeweler and the buyer?

On March 1, a bookstore emailed a publisher the following: "We have received your catalog and are interested in doing business. Do you offer any discounts to retailers?" On March 2, the publisher emailed the bookstore: "Yes, a retailer receives a 40% discount on our books if at least $500 worth of books are ordered." On March 3, the bookstore responded: "Attached is an order for $600 worth of books listed in your current catalog." On March 4, the publisher replied: "Order accepted. Please be aware, as noted in the Terms of Service in our catalog, the cost of shipping for orders of less than $1,000 is borne by the buyer." On March 5, the bookstore emailed: "Can't accept additional shipping cost. Please cancel order." The publisher did not reply. On March 6, the bookstore, having reconsidered its options, sent the following email to the publisher: "You drive a hard bargain. Please ship the books as ordered on March 3."
If the publisher does not send the books, can the publisher be liable for breach of contract?

A regional garden center regularly purchases plants from various sources to sell to its customers. In January, the garden center entered into a contract to purchase a specific quantity of fruit tree saplings from a supplier. The contract called for the saplings to be delivered in 90 days, with payment due on delivery. Coincidentally, shortly after this contract was executed, the garden center contracted with a nursery to purchase additional saplings for the upcoming spring. Unbeknownst to the garden center, the nursery was the supplier's primary source of fruit tree saplings. As a consequence of the garden center's purchase of fruit tree saplings from the nursery, the nursery ran out of saplings, and the supplier could not obtain the required number of saplings by the delivery date. Instead, the supplier delivered only half of the required number of fruit tree saplings to the garden center on the delivery date.
Has the supplier breached its contract with the garden center?

A general contractor agreed to build a refrigerated storage facility for a company that transports perishable food. A subcontractor agreed with the general contractor to install the facility's refrigeration system. Their agreement included the express condition that all pipes for the refrigeration system were to be made of solid steel. However, the subcontractor completed the job using galvanized steel pipes that he had on hand. Unlike solid steel, the galvanized steel degrades quickly upon coming into contact with the type of refrigerant used in the refrigeration system.
The general contractor discovered the substitution after the job was completed. The subcontractor, who was fully engaged out-of-state on another company's job site, declined to replace the pipes. The general contractor subsequently refused to pay the subcontractor pursuant to the contract and hired another subcontractor to replace the pipes so that the facility could be made operational.
If the subcontractor sues the general contractor for breach of contract, how is the court likely to rule?
